outside_procedure_cues: A cleartext credential matching a public default-password list would hint at universal defaults; the conceptual case reviews only IXIT.
Cleartext HTTP Basic, Telnet or MQTT logins and answering login services reveal password mechanisms; IXIT completeness cannot be judged.
Pre-installed passwords sent in cleartext can be seen and checked for form; the property route is 5.1-2-1.
TLS versions, cipher suites and certificates of authentication channels are visible in handshakes (TLS 1.3 certificates encrypted).
Repeated third-party login attempts reaching the device and its continued responses could hint at missing rate limiting; opportunistic and not used by the TS.
Answering Telnet/HTTP admin/API services expose network authentication; third-party login floods could hint at rate-limit behaviour.
Public advisory and CVE dates compared with observed firmware updates could indicate handling speed; the TS case reviews only IXIT.
Observed update traffic shows some components are updatable; the conceptual case cannot use it.
Firmware fetched over plaintext HTTP or from unexpected hosts bears on misuse resistance; the design review gives no way to use it.
Update downloads without visible user activity would suggest automatic application, i.e. simple updating; only a conceptual case exists.
Unattended update traffic suggests an automated mechanism; the conceptual case cannot use it.
Periodic requests to update endpoints after setup would show update checking; the provision has only a conceptual case, so this evidence is unused.
Gap between public vulnerability disclosure and observed firmware update arrival could indicate timeliness; the case reviews only procedures.
Update checks and downloads over plaintext HTTP or from unexpected hosts show network update paths and unauthenticated channels; signature use stays unknown.
During internet outages traffic shows reconnect behaviour, but not whether the main function survives.
SSDP/mDNS model names reveal a network-advertised model, which is not the label/UI the provision requires.
Identical credentials across same-model devices, or a public CVE on hard-coded keys for the identified model, would indicate hard-coded CSPs.
The same client certificate or credential seen on several devices of one model would suggest non-unique CSPs.
Observed handshakes (versions, suites, certificates) could be compared with IXIT if supplied; without it they only feed the conceptual catalogue check.
Server banners, User-Agent strings and TLS fingerprints may reveal library names/versions, unusable without the SO report.
Observed update traffic shows an update channel exists but says nothing about crypto replaceability.
Plaintext credentials observed in traffic would contradict the provision directly.
Plaintext credentials or tokens in traffic would contradict the provision, but this case only compares with IXIT.
Plaintext credentials to remote endpoints would contradict the provision directly.
Plaintext credentials sent to remote endpoints would contradict the provision, but this case only compares with IXIT.
Services seen answering on the LAN or WAN indicate enabled logical interfaces; completeness needs IXIT 28.
Firmware or kernel versions in SSDP, mDNS, DHCP or HTTP headers are visible unauthenticated disclosures, but undocumentedness needs IXIT.
Observed answering services (telnet, ftp, rtsp) suggest enabled services whose necessity the conceptual case cannot test.
Traffic after a genuine tamper event could be checked for restriction, but the observer cannot know detection occurred.
Plaintext personal data in traffic would contradict the provision directly.
Plaintext personal data to cloud endpoints would contradict the provision, but this case only compares with IXIT.
Plaintext sensitive personal data in traffic would contradict the provision directly.
Plaintext sensitive data (e.g. unencrypted camera streams) would contradict the provision, but this case only compares with IXIT.
After naturally occurring outages, reconnection loops, DHCP re-requests and resumed cloud sessions show how the device actually recovers.
TCP setup/teardown conformance and reconnect timing (jitter, backoff, server spread) are visible in traffic, especially after outages the observer cannot cause.
Periodic uploads to telemetry-like endpoints suggest telemetry exists, but its examination is invisible.
Observed listening services and protocols could reveal network interfaces missing from the public manual.
Retention and disposal (b,c) have no passive evidence.
Plaintext uploads of raw per-event records, where public docs describe aggregation, would hint at non-minimal collection.
Identifiers visible in plaintext uploads of data that public docs call anonymized would contradict the published claim.
